analysis.one_liner: Extends federal steel import quotas and tightens the exception process for steel buyers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one representative with zero cosponsors, was sent to a House trade subcommittee in July 1989 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have extended the Steel Import Stabilization Act — the law behind limits on steel imports — for another five years. It also would have tightened the "short supply" exception, making it harder for U.S. companies that buy steel to get permission to import specific steel products that domestic mills claimed they could supply, with penalties and a 12-month ban on future requests for buyers who misused the process.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic steel producers and their workers. Extended quotas keep foreign steel out of the U.S. market, which supports steel-industry employment and keeps domestic steel prices above world levels. The tightened short-supply rules add a second layer of protection: even when a quota technically allows some imports, steel buyers would face a higher bar and new penalties before they could bring in products domestic mills claim they can make.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Steel Import Stabilization Act, the legal basis for U.S. steel import limits, for five more years, keeping quota protection in place for domestic producers.

Tightens the short-supply exception: a buyer could only use price as a reason to import by presenting clear and convincing evidence that a domestic supplier was overcharging, and a shortage would not count just because domestic producers refuse to sell below their verified costs of production.

Adds enforcement teeth: a company that fails to use its import authorization, resells quota-protected steel, or declines to buy from a domestic supplier after a denied request is barred from making new short-supply requests for 12 months.
Bars extra imports for products under bilateral arrangements when those imports are made available solely to one domestic company, protecting the structure of the existing quota deals.

analysis.who_pays: Steel-using manufacturers — automakers, appliance makers, machinery and equipment producers, construction firms — and their workers, who pay more for their main raw material while their own products compete against imports. Consumers eventually share the cost through higher prices on steel-intensive goods. Buyers needing specific steel products domestic mills do not readily offer would also face a harder, more punitive process for getting an import exception.

drawbacks.text: Import quotas raise domestic steel prices above world levels, and steel-consuming industries employ far more workers than steel production does, so the bill's costs would land on many more paychecks than its benefits.

The tightened short-supply rules would make it substantially harder for U.S. buyers to import specific steel products they genuinely cannot get on acceptable terms — price complaints require clear and convincing evidence of overcharging, and a shortage claim fails if domestic producers simply refuse to sell below their verified costs.

Buyers face new penalties, including a 12-month ban on future import requests, for missteps such as reselling authorized imports or failing to buy domestic tonnage after a denial, adding risk to routine purchasing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a straightforward protectionist trade: concentrated gains for one heavily protected industry, paid for through higher input costs spread across every manufacturer that uses steel and the consumers who buy their products. The bill is not just a five-year extension of existing quotas — it actively tightens the escape valve buyers used to obtain steel domestic mills could nominally supply, which would make the price effects harder to avoid. The job protection for steel towns is real, but on the whole the costs to the much larger steel-consuming economy outweigh them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Ways and Means Committee's trade subcommittee and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wayne Owens of Utah introduced the bill on June 29, 1989, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which handles trade legislation.
A week later, on July 6, 1989, it was sent to the committee's Subcommittee on Trade, where no further action was taken.
The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, and the subcommittee never brought it to a vote; it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-consuming manufacturers, their workers, and consumers came out ahead because the quota extension and the tightened import-exception rules never became law. Domestic steel producers missed a chance to extend statutory protection, though the industry's basic quota regime remained in place during the period through other means.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no recorded votes, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill extends the import-quota regime that limits foreign competition and keeps domestic steel prices above world levels, and it tightens the short-supply exceptions that let buyers route around quotas. Its gain comes directly at the expense of steel buyers and consumers.

Higher steel prices flow straight into the cost structure of these firms, whose own products compete against imports, and to the workers in them. The bill's tightened short-supply rules would make it harder and riskier to obtain specific steel products from abroad.

Five more years of statutory quota authority would further restrict these firms' access to the U.S. market. Their interest in looser limits runs alongside American buyers' interest in lower steel prices.

Quota protection supports steel-industry jobs, which is the bill's genuine benefit to a group of working people. That protection is financed by higher steel prices paid by the much larger workforce in steel-consuming industries.
